title: The Agricultural Revolution
note: Farming began independently in several regions after about 10,000 BCE. Harari calls it history's biggest fraud, arguing it made most individuals worse off even as populations grew. That framing is his, and critics dispute it. Dates, crops and the origins of writing are empirical.

read.title: Who tamed whom?
text: Around 10,000 BCE, people in the Fertile Crescent, in what is now the Middle East, began to plant wheat and barley and herd sheep, goats, pigs and cattle. Farming arose separately in other places too: maize in Mesoamerica, rice and millet in China. The empirical outline is clear. Farming supported far more people per acre than foraging did, so populations grew fast.

Harari reads this as a trap. In his account, individual farmers worked harder, ate a narrower diet and caught more diseases, while wheat spread across the world. He calls the revolution history's biggest fraud and says wheat domesticated humans as much as the reverse. The luxury trap, in his telling, explains why people could not go back: each small comfort became a need.

Archaeological evidence does back part of this story, including narrower diets and new diseases from crowded settlements. But the fraud label is disputed. Critics note that more people surviving, and the cities and cultures farming made possible, are real gains, so the claim depends on how you weigh numbers against individual comfort. The word fraud also sounds like deliberate deception, though Harari himself grants that nobody planned farming; it spread slowly over generations.
Writing followed: Sumerian cuneiform began as clay-tablet records of goods, not literature.
